chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Ja'far, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Alwan, from 'Amr ibn Khalid, from Zayd ibn 'Ali, from his fathers, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said:

I and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) visited a man from the Ansar, and there was a horse of his that was killing itself (with exhaustion or age). The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Slaughter it, for you will be granted double reward for it: one for slaughtering it yourself, and one for your expectation of reward from it.' He said, 'O Messenger of Allah, do I have any share in it?' He said, 'Yes, eat and feed me.' He said, 'So he gifted the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) a thigh from it, and he ate from it and fed me.'

From him, from Musa ibn 'Umar, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Dawud ibn Kathir al-Raqqi, who said: 'I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him about the meat of the Bukt (a type of camel) and its milk, and he said, 'There is no harm with it.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: there is no harm with it (permissible)
key_terms.وَاحْتِسَابِكَ لَهُ: and your expectation of reward from it
key_terms.يُضَاعَفْ لَكَ بِهِ أَجْرَانِ: double reward will be granted for it

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on slaughtering a dying animal for food, and is the meat of the Bukt camel permissible?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Prophet’s practical wisdom in utilizing resources, where slaughtering a dying horse yields double reward (*ajran*) by combining the act of slaughter with the preservation of the animal's value. The accompanying ruling by Imam al-Hasan (or al-Sajjad, depending on the specific chain interpretation in Tusi) regarding the *Bukt* camel underscores the Shia scholarly tradition of distinguishing between specific camel breeds for permissibility of meat and milk, reflecting the detailed jurisprudence of *al-Tahdhib*. These incidents collectively illustrate the flexibility in Islamic dietary laws regarding animals not typically slaughtered for food, provided they are healthy and slaughtered correctly.
